blocks.x: The size of the gap

The Hudson's Bay closures in Winnipeg left vacancies concentrated in the city's enclosed malls. In [CBRE's 2026 outlook](https://www.cbre.com/insights/articles/whats-ahead-for-winnipeg-commercial-real-estate-in-2026), the firm's Winnipeg managing director put the Bay at about 2% of the city's retail footprint, and said landlords have managed similar losses before with Sears and Target.

That is a small share citywide, but a very large space for each mall to fill. [CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/hudsons-bay-lease-winnipeg-ym-inc-1.7599683) put the Polo Park store at 212,086 square feet over three floors and the St. Vital Centre store at 122,000 square feet over two. An anchor that size often comes with its own entrances and loading.
What Winnipeg owners are doing

[Retail Insider's February 2026 review](https://retail-insider.com/retail-insider/2026/02/winnipeg-retail-market-sees-major-investment-wave/) of Winnipeg retail showed owners still investing in the city's malls, though none of its examples is a Bay backfill:
**St. Vital Centre** was [sold to Leyad for $160.5 million](https://retail-insider.com/retail-insider/2026/02/leyad-acquires-st-vital-centre-for-160-5-million/), with Uniqlo among the new tenants.
**Kildonan Place** has a $30-million redevelopment due to finish in 2027. Dollarama doubled its store to about 16,000 square feet, and the former theatre (about 30,000 square feet) was coming down.

**Polo Park** has added tenants including London Drugs, Makers, Rodd & Gunn and [Uniqlo](https://retail-insider.com/bulletin/2026/04/uniqlo-announces-first-winnipeg-store-opening-date/), and roughly 3,700 rental units are planned on its parking lots.
These projects show the options: smaller tenants in a former anchor area, as at Polo Park's former Sears redevelopment, more food uses, and residential development on surplus land.

The former Bay spaces themselves are still open questions. At Polo Park, the mall's general manager told [CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/t-t-polo-park-winnipeg-9.7298183) in August 2026 that the former Hudson's Bay space is a greater challenge to fill and may be subdivided for multiple tenants.

At St. Vital Centre, Leyad's president told [RENX](https://renx.ca/leyad-acquire-winnipeg-st-vital-centre-160-5-million) in February 2026 that backfilling the vacant store was part of the purchase's appeal. We found no announced tenant for either space as of November 2026.
Our view: big-box space has to be broken down

Few retailers want a full department-store footprint today. Many want a smaller unit with a strong storefront and efficient back-of-house. [JLL's January 2026 outlook, as reported by Retail Insider](https://retail-insider.com/retail-insider/2026/01/hudsons-bay-boxes-likely-65-leased-within-two-years-jll/), expects about 64% of vacant Hudson's Bay space across Canada to go to multi-tenant layouts, typically three to five units of 15,000 to 40,000 square feet.
Successful repositioning usually involves:
**Selective demolition** to remove old fixtures, ceilings and non-structural walls, once older materials have been [tested for asbestos](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).
**Demising,** or dividing, the space into several units with separate entrances and services.
**New storefronts** facing the mall corridor and, where possible, the exterior.
**Flooring and finishes** suited to each tenant's brand.
**Exterior work**, including masonry and new entrances, to give each tenant visibility.

**Retail space renovation** at this scale is complex, but it can be a practical way to turn a single vacant anchor into productive space. Plan for a registered architect or professional engineer too: the [City's commercial permit guide](https://legacy.winnipeg.ca/ppd/Documents/Permits/CommercialAlterationDesignSummary/Guide-Commercial-Alteration-Design-Summary.pdf) says structural work, life-safety changes and walls between tenants generally need one.
Beyond retail
Not all former department store space will return to retail. Owners can look at:
**Fitness and entertainment**, which drive frequent visits.
**Medical and service uses**, which bring steady traffic.
**Grocery**, which anchors daily trips.
**Residential**, either on surplus parking or through redevelopment.

Each use has different requirements for floors, entrances, washrooms and permits. A change of use begins with a building permit application and ends with an [occupancy permit](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg), and it may require code upgrades.
What smaller retail landlords can learn
The same principles apply to smaller plazas and strip centres. If a large tenant leaves:
Consider dividing the space rather than waiting for a single replacement.
Invest in façades and storefronts to attract new tenants.
Think about non-retail uses that suit the location.
Get a realistic renovation budget before marketing the space, so incentives and rents can be set accordingly.
Our [vacant storefront renovation guide](/blog/vacant-storefront-renovation-winnipeg) walks through the steps for a smaller unit.
What tenants and agents should watch

For retail tenants, repositioning projects create opportunities. Newly divided anchor spaces may offer good locations within established malls, sometimes with landlord-funded improvements. Agents representing tenants should ask about the timeline for demolition and base-building work, the scope of landlord's work, and how the mall's overall redevelopment will affect traffic.

For investors, the sale of St. Vital Centre and the investments at Kildonan Place and Polo Park show confidence in Winnipeg's enclosed malls. Properties that are actively repositioned may perform better than those waiting for a single replacement anchor.
Lessons from Kildonan Place

Kildonan Place is not a former Bay site, but its redevelopment shows what a phased approach can look like. As reported in February 2026, the owner is expanding existing tenants, such as Dollarama's move to about 16,000 square feet, while demolishing the former theatre and adding a new entrance.

That combination of tenant expansion, targeted demolition and phased construction is an approach other owners can adapt at smaller scale, even for a single vacant big-box unit in a neighbourhood plaza.
The bottom line

The loss of Hudson's Bay is a challenge, but Winnipeg's mall owners are still investing. Retail space renovation that breaks big boxes into smaller, modern units, and opens the door to non-retail uses, can turn vacancies into opportunities.
